narrator.instruct: Gripping, urgent storyteller telling a true and serious history what-if, brisk and tense, never calm, never jokey.

barman.instruct: A friendly nineteenth-century saloon barman greeting a regular customer, warm and casual.

actor.instruct: A stage actor in an old comedy, booming a ridiculous insult to the back row for a big laugh, theatrical and loud.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The night Abraham Lincoln was shot, the policeman guarding his door wasn't there.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Washington, April fourteenth, eighteen sixty-five. The war is all but over. Lincoln is at Ford's Theatre, watching a comedy from a private box.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His guard: police officer John Parker. At intermission, Parker reportedly heads to the saloon next door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody knows if he came back. He wasn't at the door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Three days earlier, Lincoln had backed voting rights for some Black men. Famous actor John Wilkes Booth was reportedly in the crowd.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Just after ten, Booth climbs the stairs. He shows the footman a card, slips into the passage, and bars the door with a wooden plank.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then he waits for the biggest laugh.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One shot, hidden in the laughter.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now, what if Parker had stayed? Maybe Booth is turned away. Maybe he tries another night.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Instead, Andrew Johnson took over. He pardoned thousands of Confederates and vetoed bills protecting freed slaves. Many historians think Lincoln would have protected those rights better. Others say Congress mattered more.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And Parker? Charged with neglect of duty. The charge was dropped.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One empty chair, and a country took a different road.
